title: A glass drop that shrugs off a hammer explodes if you snap its tail
body: Drip molten glass into cold water and you get a Prince Rupert’s drop: a tadpole of glass whose head survives hammer blows and even bullets, yet turns to powder the instant its thin tail is broken. The outside freezes first; when the inside later cools and shrinks, it pulls the skin into **compression of up to 700 megapascals** while the core is left in tension. Cracks can’t grow through that squeezed skin. Snap the tail and a crack enters the stretched interior, racing through it at 1,450 to 1,900 metres per second.

slides.alt: Cross-section of a Prince Rupert’s drop: a thin outer skin marked with inward arrows for compression surrounds a core marked with outward arrows for tension, and the thin tail is labelled as the way in for a crack.
slides.caption: A squeezed skin holds a stretched core; the tail is the way in.

slides.label: compressive stress locked into the drop’s outer skin
slides.text: Roughly 7,000 times atmospheric pressure, in a layer only about a tenth of the head’s diameter thick.

slides.heading: Pressure in the air around you, and inside the drop’s skin
slides.note: Atmospheric pressure is about 0.1 MPa; the skin is squeezed roughly 7,000 times harder

slides.question: In what year did Prince Rupert of the Rhine bring the glass drops to Britain?
slides.explanation: 1660. Accounts of the drops go back to 1625 in northern Germany, and in 1661 King Charles II handed them to the Royal Society to study.

events.text: Earliest verifiable accounts, from Mecklenburg in northern Germany
Prince Rupert of the Rhine brings the drops to Britain
King Charles II hands them to the Royal Society to study

slides.question: Why does snapping the tail destroy the whole drop?
options: The tail holds the drop together
A crack reaches the stretched core
slides.explanation: The tail’s protective skin is thin, so a snap lets a crack into the interior, which is under tension. Its stored energy is released all at once and the drop shatters.
